steps.body:
Nothing changes when the chain gets longer. Peel one layer at a time, from the outside in, and multiply everything you collect.

For √((2x + 1)³): the outside is a square root, then a cube, then a linear bracket. Three layers, three factors.

explanationVariants: Three layers, three factors, multiplied together. Each factor is the derivative of one layer with the layers inside it left intact.

widget.prompt: How many factors will the derivative of √((2x + 1)³) have?

options.label: Three: outer root, cube, and inner linear rule.
options.feedback: Right. Every layer contributes exactly one factor, and the innermost is the one people drop.

options.label: Two: root and cube, with no inner rule needed.
options.feedback: The chain rule has two factors PER APPLICATION, and here it is applied twice. Layers, not applications, is the count that matters.

options.label: One: simplify first, leaving only the outer root.
options.feedback: It does simplify to (2x+1)^(3/2), which is still a chain: outer power, inner bracket. You never escape the inside.

options.label: Four: count both powers twice and the inner rule.
options.feedback: Count the layers: root, cube, linear. Three layers, three factors.

widget.prompt: A product whose factors both need a chain rule.

panels.title: Structure first
panels.body: For x²·(3x + 1)⁴, the OUTERMOST operation is a multiplication. So the product rule comes first, before anything else.

panels.title: Then each piece
panels.body: Product rule: 2x·(3x+1)⁴ + x²·[d/dx (3x+1)⁴]. That bracket is a separate, smaller problem — and it needs the chain rule: 4(3x+1)³·3 = 12(3x+1)³.

panels.title: Assemble
panels.body: f′ = 2x(3x+1)⁴ + 12x²(3x+1)³. Outermost rule first, inner rules afterwards, one at a time. Never two rules in one line.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the discipline is the outside-in order.
widget.successFeedback: Outermost operation decides the first rule. Everything inside becomes a smaller problem you solve next.

explanationVariants: At x = 0 the bracket is 1, so both powers of it are 1 — which is why the arithmetic collapses so pleasantly.

commonErrors.feedback: The second term vanishes at x = 0 (because of the factor x), but the FIRST term does not: (2·0+1)³ = 1.
That is the inner factor 6(2x+1)² at x = 0 — but it is multiplied by x, which is 0. The surviving term is (2x+1)³ = 1.
Check the product rule: 1·(2x+1)³ + x·6(2x+1)². At x = 0 that is 1 + 0.

steps.body:
Some functions refuse to be written as y = f(x) at all. x² + y² = 25 defines a whole circle, and no single formula gives y.

**Differentiate the equation anyway.** Treat y as a function of x, and every time you differentiate a y, the chain rule makes you pay a dy/dx.
The dy/dx that appears from nowhere.
explanationVariants: d/dx[y²] = 2y·(dy/dx), because y is a function of x and the chain rule demands the inner derivative.
The dy/dx is not an extra decoration — it is the inner derivative the chain rule always requires.

widget.prompt: Differentiating y² with respect to x gives what?

options.label: 2y·(dy/dx)
options.feedback: Right — y is a function of x, so the chain rule charges you its derivative. That is the whole trick of implicit differentiation.

options.label: 2y
options.feedback: That would be right if you were differentiating with respect to y. With respect to x, the chain rule adds a factor of dy/dx.

options.label: 2x
options.feedback: There is no x in y². The variable being squared is y.

options.label: 0, because y is not x.
options.feedback: y is not a constant — it changes as x changes, which is exactly why it has a derivative dy/dx.

hints: Differentiate x² + y² = 25 term by term with respect to x, remembering the chain rule on y².
You get 2x + 2y·(dy/dx) = 0. Now solve for dy/dx.
dy/dx = −x/y. Substitute the point (3, 4) and give a decimal.
explanationVariants: And that is exactly perpendicular to the radius, whose slope is 4/3 — a fact the geometry course asserted and calculus has now derived.

widget.prompt: x² + y² = 25. Find dy/dx at the point (3, 4), as a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: The sign is wrong. 2x + 2y·y′ = 0 gives y′ = −x/y, and at (3, 4) that is −3/4: the circle is FALLING there, in the upper right quadrant.
That is 4/3 — the slope of the RADIUS to that point. The tangent is perpendicular to it, so its slope is the negative reciprocal, −3/4.

steps.body: Peel the layers; pay for every y.
takeaways: Longer chains change nothing: one factor per layer, multiplied together, outside in.
When rules combine, the OUTERMOST operation decides which rule comes first.
Implicit differentiation is just the chain rule: every y you differentiate costs you a dy/dx.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: the derivatives of the function library — and the one curve that is its own derivative.

concept.body: Differentiate both sides with respect to x, exactly as normal — but every time a y appears, remember it is secretly a function of x, so the chain rule attaches a dy/dx. Then collect the dy/dx terms and solve for it like any other unknown.

explanationVariants: d/dx[y³] = 3y²·(dy/dx). The 3y² is the outside; the dy/dx is the inside.
Any power of y picks up a dy/dx when differentiated with respect to x.

widget.prompt: Differentiate y³ with respect to x.

options.label: 3y²·(dy/dx)
options.feedback: Right — outside gives 3y², and the chain rule charges you the inner derivative dy/dx.

options.label: 3y²
options.feedback: That is the derivative with respect to Y. With respect to x, the chain rule adds dy/dx.
